concepts.plain: A small chunk of text the model reads or writes, often a word or part of a word.
concepts.why: Model limits and costs are counted in tokens, not words or pages.

concepts.plain: A list of numbers that represents a token's meaning.
concepts.why: Computers compare numbers, so meaning has to become numbers first.
concepts.example: "Invoice" and "bill" end up with similar lists of numbers.

concepts.plain: One learned number inside the model. A 7B model has about 7 billion of them.
concepts.why: Parameters decide how much memory is needed to load the model.
concepts.example: At 2 bytes each, 7 billion parameters need about 13 GiB.

concepts.plain: One processing stage. Text passes through dozens of layers in order, and each refines the understanding.
concepts.why: More layers can capture more complex patterns, but cost more to run.
concepts.example: Early layers tend to capture word patterns and later layers capture higher-level meaning.

concepts.plain: How a word looks back at earlier words to work out which ones matter for it right now.
concepts.why: It lets a model connect information that is far apart in a document.
concepts.example: In "the bank of the river", attention to "river" tells the model which kind of bank it is.

concepts.plain: Think of a library. The query is the question you bring. Each key is the label on a book's spine. Each value is the content inside the book. You compare your question to the labels, then read most from the books that match best.
concepts.why: This is how attention works, and storing keys and values is usually what makes long documents expensive to process.
concepts.example: For the word "it", the query asks "which thing am I referring to?". The key of "trophy" says "I am an object". Its value supplies what the model should know about the trophy.

concepts.plain: The model's short-term memory of every earlier token. Each new token adds its keys and values, so nothing has to be recalculated.
concepts.why: It grows with document length and with the number of simultaneous users, and it is often the largest memory cost after the model itself.
concepts.example: Ten users with long documents each need their own cache, while they all share one copy of the weights.

concepts.plain: One independent "reader" in an attention layer. Several heads read the same text at once and can notice different things.
concepts.why: More heads capture more kinds of relationship, but can increase the cache.
concepts.example: One head may track grammar while another tracks who is being talked about.

concepts.plain: The part of each layer that thinks about what attention just gathered. Attention collects information and the feed-forward network processes it.
concepts.why: It holds most of a model's parameters, so it drives size and compute.
concepts.example: After attention gathers that "it" means "trophy", this step updates the token's meaning accordingly.

concepts.plain: One of many small feed-forward networks inside a layer. Only a few run for each token, like calling a few specialists instead of the whole company.
concepts.why: It lets a model hold far more knowledge without doing far more work per token.
concepts.example: A model may hold 256 experts per layer but use only 8 for any one token.

concepts.plain: A small learned scorer that decides which experts each token should go to.
concepts.why: Routing quality affects both answer quality and how evenly GPUs are loaded.
concepts.example: It scores all experts for a token and sends the token to the highest-scoring few.

concepts.plain: The most tokens the model can consider at once, covering both your input and its answer.
concepts.why: It sets how large a document can be processed in one go, and longer contexts need more memory.
concepts.example: 128K tokens is very roughly a 300-page book.

concepts.plain: Storing each parameter with fewer bits, like saving a photo at lower quality to shrink the file.
concepts.why: It cuts memory substantially, but can reduce accuracy and may need specific hardware.
concepts.example: Moving from 16-bit to 4-bit makes the weights about four times smaller.

concepts.plain: Inference is using a finished model. Training is changing its parameters.
concepts.why: Training needs far more memory and compute than inference for the same model.
concepts.example: A model that runs on a laptop may still need a data-center GPU to fine-tune.

kvDemo.intro: Select a word. Its query is compared with the key of each earlier word. The closer the match, the more of that word's value it takes in.
kvDemo.note: Hand-set numbers chosen to show the mechanism. A real model learns thousands of dimensions, and they rarely map to clear human labels like these.

words.value: An object that can be big

expertFacts.title: How does each expert learn what to do?
expertFacts.lead: Nobody assigns experts to topics. There is no "legal expert" or "math expert" set up by an engineer. Everything below happens automatically during training.

steps.title: All experts start random
steps.text: Each expert and the router begin as random numbers, with no specialty.

steps.title: The router picks a few
steps.text: For each token, the router scores the experts and sends the token to the top few.

steps.title: Only the chosen experts learn
steps.text: The model checks its prediction. The error adjusts just the experts that were used, plus the router.

steps.title: A feedback loop forms
steps.text: An expert that handled a kind of token gets better at it, so the router tends to send it more of the same. That repetition is what creates specialization.

steps.title: Balancing keeps everyone working
steps.text: Left alone, a few experts can take all the traffic while others never learn. A load-balancing penalty in training pushes the router to spread tokens more evenly.

expertFacts.finding: They usually do not line up with human subjects. When Mistral AI analyzed Mixtral's routing across ArXiv, biology and philosophy text, the distribution of experts was very similar, and it reported no obvious patterns by topic. It did find that consecutive tokens are often routed to the same experts, which suggests specialization on low-level patterns such as syntax.

source.title: Mixtral of Experts, Section 5: Routing analysis

expertFacts.implication: So you cannot choose "the finance experts" or expect to inspect one expert to learn what it knows. Judge the model by testing it on your task.
expertFacts.labIntro: This is a real, tiny mixture of experts training in your browser. It has to learn the black line, using only straight-line experts. Press Train and watch the experts claim regions on their own.
expertFacts.labNote: A toy model with one input and simple experts. It shows the learning mechanism, and real experts work in thousands of dimensions.

dense.analogy: A company where every employee works on every request.
dense.what: The classic design. Each word goes through every part of the model.
dense.why: It behaves predictably and nearly all software supports it.
dense.example: Good for small and mid-size models where simplicity matters more than peak efficiency.

faq.q: Why not make every model dense?
faq.a: Because cost rises directly with size. A very large dense model would be too slow and expensive per word.
Not automatically. The design affects cost more than it decides quality, so test on your task.

sparse-moe.analogy: A hospital with hundreds of specialists, where each patient sees only a few.
sparse-moe.what: The model is huge, but only a small slice works on each word. A router picks which slice.
sparse-moe.why: You get the knowledge capacity of a very large model at a fraction of the compute per word.
sparse-moe.example: A 400B model may use only about 13B parameters for any single word.

faq.q: If only part of it runs, can I load only that part?
faq.a: No. The router may need any expert for the next word, so all of them must stay in fast memory.

faq.q: Who decides what each expert does?
faq.a: Training does, automatically. Open the interactive lab on this page to watch it happen.

sparse-hybrid.analogy: A researcher who keeps running summary notes, and only occasionally goes back to the original documents.
sparse-hybrid.what: Most layers keep a compact summary of the text so far. A few layers do a full look-back. Expert routing is used as well.
sparse-hybrid.why: It makes very long documents affordable.
sparse-hybrid.example: Kimi K3 uses 69 summary-style layers and 24 full-attention layers.

faq.a: Exact details can blur. The periodic full-attention layers exist to recover precise lookups.
If your task needs exact quotes from long documents, test that specifically.

dense-hybrid.analogy: A team that mixes fast skimmers with a few careful readers, and everyone works on every page.
dense-hybrid.what: Different layer types are combined, but every parameter stays active.
dense-hybrid.why: It gives small models cheaper long-context handling with steady performance.
dense-hybrid.example: LFM2.5 mixes 10 convolution layers with 6 attention layers.

faq.a: Cheap layers handle most of the work, and attention layers handle the hard long-range connections.
It can be, because not every serving tool supports every layer type.

hybrid-moe.analogy: A case manager keeps a running file while specialists are called in as needed.
hybrid-moe.what: Most layers carry a fixed-size memory forward, specialists handle processing, and a few layers look back directly.
hybrid-moe.why: Very long sessions stay cheap in memory.
hybrid-moe.example: Nemotron 3 Nano combines 23 Mamba-2 layers, 23 expert layers and 6 attention layers.

faq.a: A fixed-size state updated at every word. It never grows, however long the text becomes.
That state contains information from the user's text, so it must be kept separate per user and cleared correctly.

sparse-omnimodal-moe.analogy: One specialist hospital with separate reception desks for text, images, video and audio.
sparse-omnimodal-moe.what: Different input types are converted into a common form, then processed by one expert-routed model.
sparse-omnimodal-moe.why: One deployment can handle several kinds of content.
sparse-omnimodal-moe.example: MiMo-V2.5 adds image, video and audio encoders to its sparse backbone.

faq.q: Does an image use up context?
faq.a: Yes. Each image, frame or audio clip becomes many tokens and takes room from the context.

faq.q: Do all these models accept all inputs?
faq.a: No. Check the exact checkpoint, because capabilities vary.

sparse-moe-causal-encoder-decoder.analogy: One team writes a shared briefing, and a second team uses it instead of each person taking their own notes.
sparse-moe-causal-encoder-decoder.what: The layers are split into two halves. The first half produces a shared memory that the second half reads.
sparse-moe-causal-encoder-decoder.why: Sharing that memory reduces the total cache.
sparse-moe-causal-encoder-decoder.example: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash uses 20 encoder and 20 decoder layers.

faq.a: Each word can only see words before it, never ones after it, which is required when generating text.
Rare. Only one model in this catalog uses it, so check runtime support first.

recurrent.analogy: Someone listening to a long story who can only keep a fixed set of notes.
recurrent.what: No look-back at all. Each word updates a fixed-size memory, then the model moves on.
recurrent.why: Memory use stays constant however long the input is.
recurrent.example: xLSTM uses 32 recurrent layers with a matrix memory.

faq.q: Can it recall exact text from far back?
faq.a: Only what survived in its notes, which is why exact recall is harder than with attention.
Attention became the standard, so far less software and tuning exists for recurrent models.

linear.analogy: Keeping a running summary instead of re-reading the whole book.
linear.what: Each word updates a compact summary, and lookups read from that summary.
linear.why: Memory stays flat as documents grow.
linear.example: Useful for million-token documents, combined with some full-attention layers.

faq.q: What are keys and values here?
faq.a: They still exist, but they are folded into one summary instead of being stored per word.
Similar items can blur together in the summary, so exact recall weakens.

statespace.analogy: A notepad of fixed size that you keep rewriting as you read.
statespace.what: A fixed-size state is updated at each word and the output is read from it.
statespace.why: Long inputs cost almost no extra memory.
statespace.example: Mamba layers in the Nemotron models.

faq.a: Yes, gradually. Older information tends to fade unless the model learned to keep it.
Not strictly, though it can be expressed in a closely related mathematical form.

recurrent.analogy: A notebook with gates that decide what to write, keep and read.
recurrent.what: Learned gates control what enters and leaves a memory matrix at every word.
recurrent.why: Memory is constant for any length of text.

faq.a: A learned dial between 0 and 1 that controls how much information passes.
Mainly for streaming or research uses, since production support is limited.

convolution.analogy: Reading through a small sliding magnifying glass.
convolution.what: Each word is mixed with its few immediate neighbours.
convolution.why: It is extremely cheap and needs almost no memory.
convolution.example: LFM models use these blocks for local patterns.

faq.a: Not on its own. Attention layers do that.
The small set of learned weights that defines how neighbours are mixed.

mtp.analogy: A typist who guesses the next few words, then checks them all at once.
mtp.what: Extra outputs predict several future tokens from the same internal state.
mtp.why: Correct guesses can speed up generation.
mtp.example: If the next three tokens are guessed correctly, you get three tokens for about the price of one step.

faq.q: What if the guess is wrong?
faq.a: It is discarded and generation continues normally, so only some compute is wasted.
With proper verification it should not, because guesses are only kept when confirmed.

moe.analogy: A hospital where a triage nurse sends each patient to a few specialists.
moe.what: One big processing block is replaced by many small experts. A router chooses a few for each word.
moe.why: Capacity grows without a matching growth in work per word.
moe.example: 256 experts per layer, with 8 used per word.

faq.q: How does an expert get its specialty?
faq.a: It emerges during training, as explained in the walkthrough and lab on this page.

faq.q: Can I see what an expert knows?
faq.a: Not easily. Experts rarely match human subjects like law or biology.

faq.q: Why does it need so much memory if few experts run?
faq.a: Any expert could be needed for the next word, so all of them must stay loaded.

window.analogy: Mostly reading the last few pages, with an occasional check of the whole book.
window.what: Most layers only look at recent words. Every few layers, one looks at everything.
window.why: It cuts memory for long documents.
window.example: A 5:1 pattern has five local layers for every global layer.

faq.q: Do facts outside the window vanish?
faq.a: No, but they reach local layers only through the global layers.
Questions that depend on details far away in a long document.

sparse.analogy: Using the book's index to jump to the few relevant pages.
sparse.what: A cheap scorer picks which earlier words matter, and full attention runs only on those.
sparse.why: It reduces compute on long documents.

faq.q: What if the scorer misses something?
faq.a: That layer cannot use it, so selection quality matters.
Mostly compute. Keys often still need to be stored.

gated.analogy: A volume knob on each reader's contribution.
gated.what: A learned gate decides how much of each attention result passes through.
gated.why: The model can effectively say "nothing relevant here".
gated.example: Plain attention must always pay attention to something, but a gate can turn it down to almost nothing.

faq.a: It removes pressure to dump attention on meaningless tokens, a behaviour known as attention sinks.
No. It mainly improves behaviour and adds a small cost.

mla.analogy: Filing one compact index card per page, and rebuilding the details when needed.
mla.what: Instead of storing keys and values for every head, it stores one small compressed vector per word.
mla.example: DeepSeek's models use this to handle long contexts with less memory.

faq.q: What are keys and values here?
faq.a: They are reconstructed from the compact vector when attention runs.
It needs specialized software to run fast.

gqa.analogy: Eight researchers sharing two copies of the catalog instead of each keeping their own.
gqa.what: Many query heads share a smaller set of stored keys and values.
gqa.why: Less memory for almost the same quality, so it is the most common design here.
gqa.example: 16 query heads sharing 4 key-value heads uses a quarter of the cache.

faq.a: The key is a label describing a word, and the value is the information it offers. See the interactive example on this page.

faq.q: Why do they matter for cost?
faq.a: They are stored for every word, in every layer, for every user. That adds up quickly.

mha.analogy: Eight researchers, each keeping a complete personal catalog.
mha.what: The original attention. Each head stores its own keys and values.

faq.a: The key is a label describing a word, and the value is the information it offers. See the interactive example on this page.

faq.q: Why have newer designs replaced it?
faq.a: Storing a full set per head is expensive for long documents.

qknorm.analogy: Making sure nobody can win a vote just by shouting.
qknorm.what: Queries and keys are scaled to a consistent size before they are compared.
qknorm.example: Without it, a few very large values can take over all the attention.

faq.q: Should this affect my choice of model?
faq.a: Rarely. It is an internal stability detail.
Software must implement it exactly, or quality can quietly degrade.

position.what: Tells the model the order of words, often by rotating their numbers by an angle.
position.why: Without order, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look alike.
position.example: RoPE uses rotation, so the angle between two words reflects how far apart they are.

faq.q: Why would a model have none?
faq.a: Some layers rely on only seeing earlier words, which already gives some sense of order.
It can. Stretching context beyond what the model trained on usually lowers quality.
